title: DNase-Seq/DNasel-Seq
scope: Illumina family-level explanatory drawing plus separately qualified, text-supported variants. The visible route is active chromatin → DNase I digestion → isolation of trimmed complexes → DNA extraction → DNA. The leftmost titled chromatin icon is descriptive, with no incoming/outgoing transfer arrow establishing another operation; its yellow DNA highlighting has no legend and is not assigned a chemical modification. The yellow digestion-panel symbols are interpreted in the context of the DNase I label, not as products or defined chemical structures. There are no depicted alternative branches. Catalogue sequencing is a text-only continuation; Pico-Seq, the tagged-AbrB GeF-seq implementation and the cited liDNase-seq variant are independent primary-supported routes, not transfers or chronological steps between methods. The unnamed formaldehyde variation in the card specifies stabilization before digestion and reversal before DNA purification, but does not identify a further protocol; GeF-seq below provides the inspected implementation with a resolved capture interface. Neither bibliography nor CMS date establishes invention or priority.

operations.label: DNase I digestion
operations.description: Act on DNA within active chromatin. Accessible DNA is cleaved while the schematic retains DNA associated with protein-like grey complexes; subsequent trimming/isolation separates those complexes.
operations.mechanism: DNase I endonuclease digestion of chromatin DNA; protein-associated DNA can resist cleavage. The drawing does not define reaction-end chemistry.
operations.information_effect: Differential cleavage/protection relates genomic DNA fragments to the original accessibility and protein-occupancy context; DNase I is a reagent, not the measured analyte.

operations.label: Sequencing (catalogue text; not drawn)
operations.description: Use the extracted DNA for the sequencing readout described by the card. Library construction is not resolved for this unqualified drawing and is not decomposed into an assumed preparation sequence.
operations.information_effect: The card links DNA sequences to genomic protein-location information. For ordinary DNase-seq, protection is inferred within larger hypersensitive regions; it does not mean every mapped read is a protected binding-site fragment. Definitive protein identity requires orthogonal binding evidence. The card warns of sequence dependence and incomplete hypersensitive-site coverage; cleavage or survival is not perfect biological specificity.

method_scopes.rationale: The slash-grouped card names and the DNase-Seq image title are treated as one catalogue family, not evidence of two distinct chemistries. The first three operations preserve exactly the depicted retained-complex route; sequencing is a text-only continuation. The drawing does not identify the implementation behind Isolate trimmed complexes. Boyle’s abstract establishes an open-chromatin/DHS mapping assay but cannot assign this capture step. Conventional DNase-seq is interpreted through preferential cleavage and local footprints, not a universal assertion that protected complexes supply all reads. The card’s unnamed formaldehyde variation places stabilization before digestion and reversal before purification; it is not imposed on the unmarked image. GeF-seq below resolves a particular crosslinked capture route.

method_scopes.rationale: The card calls its high-sensitivity reference scDNase-seq; Jin et al. name their circular-carrier single/few-cell DHS assay Pico-Seq. These labels are linked to that cited implementation. The route recovers released small hypersensitive DNA with a circular carrier, then makes and sequences a preferentially amplified library. It does not inherit the diagram’s isolated-protected-complex selection or GeF-seq affinity capture. FFPE is also an application in the paper, but no FFPE-recovery branch is shown in the supplied diagram or assigned to this single/few-cell route.

Its cited primary implementation uses formaldehyde-fixed B. subtilis expressing tagged AbrB, enzyme access, in situ DNase I digestion, cobalt-bead affinity recovery, reversal and short-insert library sequencing. This is not simply a crosslinking add-on to a generic DHS fragment library.
